$comment: THE SHARED FIXTURE — docs/PRODUCT_v0.3.md §5.2, 'the honest residual, not buried'.
C20 moved the derived-state arithmetic to the server, so it now exists TWICE: in Kotlin
(domain/model/User.kt — Leveling, and the client's own reading of a fact set) and in
TypeScript (functions/src/projection.ts). That is a second IMPLEMENTATION, and two
implementations of one rule can disagree. §5.2 accepted the duplication — avoiding it costs
the offline win entirely — on one condition: that both are pinned by ONE fixture both test
layers read.
This is that file. It is NOT two copies of the same numbers; it is one copy read from two
sides. Its readers:
- functions/test/projection.test.mjs   (node:test, ../shared-fixtures/derived-state.json)
- app/src/test/java/com/idomarhaim/goalpilot/derived/DerivedStateFixtureTest.kt (JUnit)
Both resolve it by walking up from their own module directory, so neither owns it.
ADDING A CASE IS THE POINT. A number that disagreed in the wild belongs here as a case,
not as a fix in one language. If you change the level curve or the points rule, change it
here first and let both suites go red.
SHAPE. Every case gives the FACTS and the EXPECTED PROJECTION. Facts are what the user did;
the projection is what the server stores. Nothing here stores a level: publicProfiles.level
was deleted by C20 (a stored function of points in the same document), so `level` below is
asserted as a COMPUTED value on both sides and never as a written field.
#55 SPLIT `facts` IN TWO, AND BOTH HALVES ARE REAL.
- `completionFacts` is the LIVE shape (§1.4): a banked completion at
users/{uid}/completionFacts/{taskId}, carrying the INPUTS -- minutes and difficulty --
from which points are computed as round(minutes / 3) x difficulty. Never a number.
- `tasks` is the PRE-#55 shape: `done` + a stored `points` on the task document. #55
writes no backfill, so a task completed before it keeps that shape until something
writes it, and the projection must keep counting it or every lifetime total collapses
on deploy. It is the old source, draining -- not a second source of truth.
A task id appearing in BOTH is counted once, from its fact: that is the task that has been
re-ticked since the migration, and the fact is what was actually banked.
2026-08-25 ADDED `windowCases`, AND THE GAP IT CLOSES IS THE ONE THIS FILE EXISTS FOR.
`scoringWindow` is the rule that decides WHICH entries a challenge counts, it exists in
Kotlin (Challenge.scoringWindowFor) and TypeScript (derived.ts), and until today it was
pinned by NOTHING here -- while being the likeliest of all of them to diverge, because
the two are written in different shapes (an if/else against a nested ternary).
It changed in both languages on 2026-08-25 (a dated challenge scores its own window, so
a RETROACTIVE race can be joined after it ended), which is exactly the moment the header
above says to add cases first and let both suites go red.

pointsCases.name: legacy: tasks exist but none are done — an undone task contributes nothing
legacy: only the done ones are summed
legacy: exactly on a level boundary — L2 begins at 100, inclusive
legacy: one point below a boundary stays on the lower level
legacy: L4 begins at 600, and a big pile does not skip past it
legacy: a negative task value cannot drag the total below zero
legacy: a task with no points field counts as zero, not as a crash
legacy: idempotence, stated as data — the same fact set gives the same number
$note: It models the only way projection could double-credit — two facts of equal weight —
and pins that the answer is arithmetic over whatever the fact set holds, never an
accumulator. Run the projection twice on the real set and you get 240 both times;
that is what 'structurally idempotent' means and why FieldValue.increment stays
rejected (§5.2).
THE TWO IDS WERE BOTH `t1` UNTIL #55, with a note explaining that two rows with one id
cannot exist in Firestore and that the case therefore modelled nothing real. It is
`t1`/`t2` now because the projection is KEYED BY TASK ID -- that is how it counts a
re-ticked task once rather than twice -- so the old shape collapsed to 120 and the
case would have been asserting the de-duplication instead of the arithmetic. The
de-duplication has its own case below, where it is the point.

pointsCases.name: #55 the anchor survives: 30 routine minutes are still worth 10
$note: §1.4 inverts a constant rather than adding one, precisely so this number does not
move. If this case ever goes red, the inversion has re-priced the user's history.

pointsCases.name: #55 the three multipliers, on one duration
#55 the ceiling is 240 and nothing clamps to it
$note: 480 is the storable duration maximum and DEMANDING is x1.5, so 240 is what the
formula YIELDS rather than a constant anybody wrote down. §1.4's 'the levelling
ceiling rises 50 to 240' is this arithmetic, and the old 5..50 cap would have made it
unreachable.

pointsCases.name: #55 the floor is gone: a 15-minute light task is worth 4, not 5
$note: round(15/3) = 5, x0.75 = 3.75, rounded = 4. The old MIN_POINTS = 5 would have raised
it, which is half of what 'the 5..50 cap is deleted' means.

pointsCases.name: #55 an unknown difficulty is ROUTINE — the neutral value, not an error
$note: ROUTINE is x1.0, so an unreadable judgement prices the task on its minutes alone —
which is what a task nobody judged is worth. Mirrors Difficulty.fromName.

pointsCases.name: #55 migration: banked facts and un-migrated legacy tasks are summed together
$note: The case the deploy turns on. #55 writes no backfill, so on the day it ships every
account is exactly this: some completions banked, most not. Reading only the new
collection would have silently zeroed the older half of everybody's lifetime total.

pointsCases.name: #55 migration: a re-ticked task is counted once, from its fact
$note: Same task id in both halves. The FACT wins — it is what was actually banked at the
tick, and the legacy fields are what the migrating write is about to clear. Summing
both would double-credit exactly the tasks a user touches most.

pointsCases.name: #55 migration: a legacy point value round-trips to itself, losslessly
$note: 40 legacy points reconstruct to 40 x 3 = 120 minutes at ROUTINE (see
TaskDuration.legacyMinutesFromPoints), which prices back at round(120/3) x 1.0 = 40.
So the two rows here are the SAME completion read on either side of the migration,
and they are worth the same. That identity is why #55 needs no backfill write.

scoreCases.name: a report of zero is a report, not an absence
the latest absolute report is the score — the UI reports a total, not a delta
a negative report is clamped rather than stored
no report at all leaves the row alone
$note: score: null means DO NOT WRITE. Deleting the report fact (leaving the challenge, or an
undo) must not silently zero a standing other people are reading — the projection
writes nothing and the last reported number stands until the row itself is deleted.

windowCases.name: a dated challenge scores its own window, whoever joined when
RETROACTIVE: joining a week that already ended still scores that week
$why: Ido, 2026-08-25: a steps race for last week, invited a friend, she accepts
today. Under the pre-2026-08-25 rule the lower bound was max(joinedAt,
startAt) = today, which is past endAt, so includes() admitted nothing and the
race scored zero for everybody. This case is that bug, pinned in both
languages so neither can drift back to it.

windowCases.name: an OPEN-ENDED challenge still bounds at joinedAt -- §6's own case
$why: What §6's joinedAt rule was actually protecting: 'joining with a year-old goal
imports a year of history nobody raced for'. With no startAt there is no other
floor, so this half of the rule is unchanged and must stay unchanged.

windowCases.name: a start date with no end is open at the top, bounded at the start
an absent challenge and an absent joinedAt are zero, never NaN
$why: A NaN bound would include nothing at all and read as 'this challenge scores
zero' -- the same symptom as the retroactive bug, arriving from the other side.
